A function $P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]$ assigning probabilities to events and satisfying the axioms

questions.explanation: A probability function (measure) has domain the event space $\mathcal F$ and codomain $[0,1]$, with $P(\varnothing)=0$, $P(S)=1$, and countable additivity over disjoint events.
questions.source_support: The definition states that a probability function is $P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]$ assigning probabilities to events and satisfying the axioms.

questions.source_support: The examples say a fair die probability function assigns probability one sixth to each single-face event.

options: To make every event equally likely
To make the assigned chances consistent with nonnegativity, certainty, and additivity
To ensure all sample spaces are finite
To force every event to have probability one, regardless of the specific input chosen.
questions.explanation: The axioms (nonnegativity, $P(S)=1$, additivity) guarantee the assigned chances are coherent and free of contradiction.
questions.source_support: The definition requires the probability function to satisfy the axioms of probability.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Equally-likely is a special modeling choice (uniform), not a requirement of the axioms.
The axioms allow countable sample spaces too; finiteness is not enforced.
If every event had probability $1$, two disjoint events would have union exceeding $1$, breaking additivity.
